newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian child sex scandal report to parliament.
newsitem.headline: Belgian child sex scandal report to parliament.

text.p: A Belgian parliamentary commission will on Tuesday hand to party leaders the results of six months of hearings into bungling and worse by authorities investigating the country's child abduction and murder scandals.
As they do so, police will be digging again for evidence and possibly bodies at an abandoned mining complex in the Jumet suburb of the central city of Charleroi.
They dug without finding anything at the mine in December and January.

A leak of a draft of the commission's report into the activities of convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux found that police and magistrates investigating the disappearances were inhumane, inept, inefficient and ill trained.

The arrest of Dutroux last August followed by the rescue of two sexually-abused girls from a makeshift dungeon in one of his houses and the discovery of the bodies of four more girls profoundly unsettled the nation.
Two of the girls, both aged eight, had starved to death. Dutroux has been charged with murder.
Last month the body of another eight-year-old Belgian-born Moroccan girl was found stuffed into a steel trunk in the basement of a Brussels garage near her home.
Convicted child abuser Patrick Derochette has been charged with illegal imprisonment and rape leading to her death.
As investigations continued, evidence began to come to light of police bungling, judicial rivalry and the failure of communications on a scale that most Belgians found unbelievable.
Suspicions began to circulate that Dutroux and his accomplices had benefitted from protection by people in high places -- a view reinforced by the televised hearings of the parliamentary commission.
Between October and March the parliamentarians interviewed 110 witnesses from magistrates to police and parents.
The hearings often topped the viewing figures as people watched magistrates and police accusing each other, having memory lapses and changing their stories.
The leaked extracts published last Wednesday by listings magazine Telemoustique are a catalogue of errors.

Investigators were slow to get onto the cases, ignored vital evidence, were cold and dismissive towards the parents, jealously guarded key information, had insufficient resources and used them badly and in a completely uncoordinated manner.

In October more than 250,000 people took to the streets of Brussels in support of the parents and child victims, and to demonstrate their disgust at the abject failure of the country's justice system.
The government immediately promised wide-ranging reforms of the police and magistrature as well as more support for the victims and their families.
But the mood in Belgium is ugly. Unless the reforms bear fruit and unless some heads roll there is every chance that there will be a repeat of the October march -- only this time bigger and angrier.

The commission report, to be debated in parliament on Wednesday and Thursday, will highlight failures in the system and is expected to name some of the key players who failed to do their jobs properly.
However, it will not be the definitive work on the matter.
The commission has been given until September 30 to follow its theory that there may have been highly placed people pulling strings to interfere with the investigations.
It is that report that Belgians will be watching like hawks.
